h1:
Prasat Hin Phan Yot
A Limestone Lagoon in the Satun Sea
intro: Picture a wall of jagged limestone spires rising straight out of the sea, with a narrow gap you can paddle a kayak through to reach a quiet little lagoon hidden inside. That's Prasat Hin Phan Yot, on Khao Yai Island — one of the most talked-about photo spots for anyone visiting Satun. The rock isn't ordinary stone either: it's limestone roughly 450–500 million years old, inside Thailand's UNESCO Satun Global Geopark. We'll walk you through how to get there, what it costs, when to go, and what's worth knowing before you commit to the trip.

blocks.html: Prasat Hin Phan Yot sits on Khao Yai Island, within Mu Ko Phetra National Park in Satun province, about 3 km out to sea from Pak Bara Pier. What sets it apart from other islands is the limestone wall: sea and wind have eroded it over millennia into a row of sharp spires that look like a castle, with a small opening in the middle that lets a boat slip through to a lagoon — an enclosed pool of water ringed by rock on all four sides. It's a rare sight, and it sticks with people who've actually seen it.

blocks.text: Why this place feels so unusual

blocks.html: The appeal of Prasat Hin Phan Yot is the quiet and the sheer scale of the rock. As you paddle through the narrow gap, the sound of the waves outside slowly fades until all you hear is your paddle dipping into the water of a lagoon walled in by towering stone. Sunlight slants down in shafts through the pointed peaks, and it feels like you've slipped into another world. The limestone here formed during the Cambrian–Ordovician period, roughly 450–500 million years ago. The harder rock still stands as sharp spires, while the softer rock has been eroded away — which is how it got the shape you see today.

items: A lagoon walled in by rock — paddle through the gap and you reach a still pool of water ringed by jagged limestone spires on every side.
Rock 450–500 million years old — dating to the Cambrian period, it's one of the geological highlights of the Satun Geopark.
The Dragon Crest sandbar — a long ridge of sand and rock that surfaces at low tide so you can walk it, near Hin Ngam Bay — another photo stop on the same route.
The island's ecosystem — mangroves, shallow coral, and shorebirds, which you'll often get to look at along the way.

blocks.text: How to get there and where to catch the boat

blocks.html: You can't visit Prasat Hin Phan Yot on your own — you have to go with a tour, because it involves a boat ride out to sea and then a kayak paddle into the lagoon. The main departure point is the Pak Bara–Ban Bo Jet Luk area in La-ngu district, where local community tourism groups run the visits. You drive to the pier, park, then take a community boat out for about 15–30 minutes to reach Khao Yai Island, where you switch to a kayak and paddle through the rock gap into the lagoon.

items: By air — the nearest airport is Hat Yai, then a road transfer to Satun town and Pak Bara Pier, around 2–2.5 hours in total.
By car — from Satun town to Pak Bara Pier in La-ngu district is about 1 hour on good roads, with parking at the pier.
Community boat — departs from Pak Bara/Ban Bo Jet Luk to Khao Yai Island, a short ride, then you switch to a kayak into the lagoon.

blocks.title: The tides matter a lot here
blocks.html: Paddling into the lagoon is only possible during certain windows when the water level is just right. If the tide is too high, the gap shrinks and is hard to slip through; if it's too low, you can't paddle in at all. That's why the community tour times shift with the daily tide schedule rather than running at fixed hours. Because of this, you need to book ahead and ask for a slot when the tide is right — don't just walk in, because there may be no paddle-in slot available that day.

The Prasat Hin Phan Yot tour is a community-run half-day to full-day trip. Prices depend on the package and group size; from what we've checked, they range from a basic option around 800 THB per person up to a full-service package around 1,500 THB per person. The price usually covers the boat, kayak, a local guide, a life vest, one meal, drinking water, and fruit. We'd suggest asking the operator directly before you go, since prices and time slots change with the season and the tide schedule.

blocks.title: Straight talk
blocks.html: The 800–1,500 THB range is what we've seen across several operators, but the real price comes down to group size — the more people you go with, the cheaper it works out per head. If you go solo or as a pair, you may have to wait to join a group or pay more. Better to contact them ahead and ask clearly than to gamble on it when you arrive.

blocks.text: When's the best time to go

blocks.html: The calm season, when the sea is settled and good for boats, runs roughly November–April: less swell, clearer water, and easy kayaking. The monsoon runs from around mid-May to mid-October, with strong waves and plenty of rain, when Mu Ko Phetra National Park may close or suspend boat departures. Before you go, check the park's announcements and ask the community group whether trips are running. Most importantly, keep an eye on the tide schedule too, since paddling into the lagoon is only possible when the water is at the right level.

blocks.text: A half-day plan for Khao Yai Island and Prasat Hin Phan Yot

blocks.html: Most people do this as a half-day trip — some make it a day trip from Satun town, or tack it onto a boat ride out to other islands. Below is a sample morning timeline; adjust it to whatever tide window the community schedules for you.

blocks.label: Morning slot
blocks.title: Khao Yai Island + Prasat Hin Phan Yot

items.activity: Arrive at Pak Bara/Ban Bo Jet Luk pier, check in with the community group, collect your life vest
items.note: Come a little before the meeting time, allowing for parking and the briefing

items.activity: Board the boat out to Khao Yai Island, passing island views and mangroves along the way
items.note: Bring a waterproof camera or a dry bag for your phone

items.activity: Switch to a kayak and paddle through the rock gap into the Prasat Hin Phan Yot lagoon
items.note: Listen to the guide about the tide timing, and paddle single file

items.activity: Take photos in the lagoon, stop by the Dragon Crest or Hin Ngam Bay if the tide is low enough
items.note: Don't take rocks or shells home — this is a national park

items.activity: Paddle back, board the boat to shore, eat with the community
items.note: The full-day package usually includes this meal

blocks.label: After that
blocks.title: If you still have time the same day

items.activity: Drive inland to Wang Sai Thong Waterfall for a cooling swim
items.note: The waterfall closes around 16:00, so go early afternoon

items.activity: Head back to Satun town for dinner — roti and pulled tea, or seafood
items.note: Satun town has plenty of food at friendly prices

blocks.text: What to know before you go

items: You must go with a community tour — you can't get in on your own. Contact the community tourism groups around Pak Bara–Ban Bo Jet Luk in advance.
Pack waterproof gear — phone, camera, and valuables should go in a dry bag, since you'll likely get wet kayaking.
Wear shoes that can get wet — strapped sandals or water shoes make walking on rock and getting in and out of the boat easier than loose flip-flops.

The rock is more fragile than it looks — parts of it have collapsed in the past, forcing temporary closures. Paddle behind the guide, don't grab or climb the rock, and check that it's open as usual before you go.

blocks.title: Getting the shot
blocks.html: The morning light in the lagoon is softer and quieter than in the afternoon, making it the best time for photos. If you want a shot of a kayak framed by the pointed rocks, tell your guide you'd like to stop at the mouth of the gap, then wait for the moment after the other boats have paddled past.

faq.q: Can I visit Prasat Hin Phan Yot on my own?
faq.a: No — you have to go with a community tour, because it involves a boat ride out to Khao Yai Island and then a kayak paddle through the rock gap into the lagoon. The community tourism groups around Pak Bara–Ban Bo Jet Luk run the visits. Book ahead and ask for a slot when the tide is right.

faq.q: How much does a Prasat Hin Phan Yot tour cost?
faq.a: It ranges from a half-day package starting around 800 THB per person up to a full-service full-day package around 1,500 THB per person. The price usually covers the boat, kayak, guide, life vest, one meal, and drinking water. The real cost depends on group size and season, so we'd suggest asking the operator directly.

faq.q: When's the best time to visit Prasat Hin Phan Yot?
faq.a: November–April is when the sea is calm and the water clear — the best time for boats and kayaking. Mid-May to mid-October is the monsoon, with strong waves, when Mu Ko Phetra National Park may suspend boat trips. Check the announcements before you go, and watch the tide schedule too, since you can only paddle into the lagoon when the water is at the right level.

faq.q: How long does a Prasat Hin Phan Yot trip take?
faq.a: Most are half-day trips. From boarding the boat, kayaking, and taking photos to getting back to shore takes around 3–4 hours. Many people do it as a day trip from Satun town and still fit in a waterfall or head back into town the same day.

faq.q: Where is Prasat Hin Phan Yot and how do I get there?
faq.a: It's on Khao Yai Island, within Mu Ko Phetra National Park in Satun province, about 3 km out to sea from Pak Bara Pier. Make your way to Pak Bara Pier in La-ngu district (about 1 hour from Satun town), then take a community boat and continue by kayak.
